article.title: The Problem of Scarce Resources
glossary: * OECD: Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development

items.sentence_raw: The problem of how health-care resources should be allocated or apportioned, so that they are distributed in both the most just and most efficient way, is not a new one.
items.explain: Q28: The passage says *'Every health system in an economically developed society is faced with the need to decide'* how to share health-care resources. This means the problem is **shared by every economically developed country**, which matches heading **iv**.

items.sentence_raw: Every health system in an economically developed society is faced with the need to decide (either formally or informally)
items.explain: Q28: The passage says *'Every health system in an economically developed society is faced with the need to decide'* how to share health-care resources. This means the problem is **shared by every economically developed country**, which matches heading **iv**.

items.sentence_raw: what proportion of the community's total resources should be spent on health-care; how resources are to be apportioned; what diseases and disabilities and which forms of treatment are to be given priority; which members of the community are to be given special consideration in respect of their health needs; and which forms of treatment are the most cost-effective.

What is new is that, from the 1950s onwards, there have been certain general changes in outlook about the finitude of resources as a whole and of health-care resources in particular, as well as more specific changes regarding the clientele of health-care resources and the cost to the community of those resources.

Thus, in the 1950s and 1960s, there emerged an awareness in Western societies that resources for the provision of fossil fuel energy were finite and exhaustible and that the capacity of nature or the environment to sustain economic development and population was also finite.
In other words, we became aware of the obvious fact that there were 'limits to growth'.
The new consciousness that there were also severe limits to health-care resources was part of this general revelation of the obvious.
items.explain: Q32: The passage says a *'new consciousness that there were also severe limits to health-care resources'* appeared. This new awareness happened in the 1950s and 1960s, which is **between 1950 and 1980**, so the answer is **B**.

items.sentence_raw: Looking back, it now seems quite incredible that in the national health systems that emerged in many countries in the years immediately after the 1939-45 World War, it was assumed without question that all the basic health needs of any community could be satisfied, at least in principle; the 'invisible hand' of economic progress would provide.
items.explain: Q34: The passage says that right after the 1939-45 World War, people assumed *'the invisible hand of economic progress would provide'* all health needs. This belief existed **between 1945 and 1950**, so the answer is **A**.

items.sentence_raw: However, at exactly the same time as this new realization of the finite character of health-care resources was sinking in, an awareness of a contrary kind was developing in Western societies: that people have a basic right to health-care as a necessary condition of a proper human life.

Like education, political and legal processes and institutions, public order, communication, transport and money supply, health-care came to be seen as one of the fundamental social facilities necessary for people to exercise their other rights as autonomous human beings.
items.explain: Q29: The passage says health-care is *'one of the fundamental social facilities necessary for people to exercise their other rights'*. This shows a direct **connection between health-care and other human rights**, so the answer is **i**.

items.sentence_raw: People are not in a position to exercise personal liberty and to be self-determining if they are poverty-stricken, or deprived of basic education, or do not live within a context of law and order.
In the same way, basic health-care is a condition of the exercise of autonomy.
items.explain: Q36: The passage says *'basic health-care is a condition of the exercise of autonomy'* — **'autonomy'** means personal liberty and independence. This directly contradicts the question, which says they have ***never*** been linked. So the answer is **NO**.

items.sentence_raw: Although the language of 'rights' sometimes leads to confusion, by the late 1970s it was recognized in most societies that people have a right to health-care (though there has been considerable resistance in the United States to the idea that there is a formal right to health-care).
It is also accepted that this right generates an obligation or duty for the state to ensure that adequate health-care resources are provided out of the public purse.
items.explain:
Q30: The passage says the right to health-care *'generates an obligation or duty for the state to ensure that adequate health-care resources are provided'*. This is exactly about **the role of the state in health-care**, so the answer is **iii**.

Q35: The passage says it is accepted that the state has a duty to ensure health-care, and this was recognized *'by the late 1970s'*. This acceptance happened **between 1950 and 1980**, so the answer is **B**.

items.sentence_raw: The state has no obligation to provide a health-care system itself, but to ensure that such a system is provided.
Put another way, basic health-care is now recognized as a 'public good', rather than a 'private good' that one is expected to buy for oneself.

As the 1976 declaration of the World Health Organization put it: "The enjoyment of the highest attainable standard of health is one of the fundamental rights of every human being without distinction of race, religion, political belief, economic or social condition."
As has just been remarked, in a liberal society basic health is seen as one of the indispensable conditions for the exercise of personal autonomy.

Just at the time when it became obvious that health-care resources could not possibly meet the demands being made upon them, people were demanding that their fundamental right to health-care be satisfied by the state.
items.explain: Q37: The passage says *'Just at the time when it became obvious that health-care resources could not possibly meet the demands... people were demanding that their fundamental right to health-care be satisfied'*. This means the two realizations happened at the **same time**, so the answer is **YES**.

items.sentence_raw: The second set of more specific changes that have led to the present concern about the distribution of health-care resources stems from the dramatic rise in health costs in most OECD* countries, accompanied by large-scale demographic and social changes which have meant, to take one example, that elderly people are now major (and relatively very expensive) consumers of health-care resources.
items.explain:
Q31: The passage talks about *'the dramatic rise in health costs'* and *'large-scale demographic and social changes'* that affect health-care today. These are all examples of **the impact of recent change**, so the answer is **v**.

Q33: The passage mentions *'the dramatic rise in health costs in most OECD countries'* as a recent change. This sharp rise happened from 1960 to 1980, which is **between 1950 and 1980**, so the answer is **B**.

Q38: The passage says the rise in health costs was *'accompanied by large-scale demographic and social changes'*, giving the example of elderly people. **'Demographic changes'** means **population changes**, so the answer is **YES**.

items.sentence_raw: Thus in OECD countries as a whole, health costs increased from 3.8% of GDP* in 1960 to 7% of GDP in 1980, and it has been predicted that the proportion of health costs to GDP will continue to increase.
(In the US the current figure is about 12% of GDP, and in Australia about 7.8% of GDP.)

As a consequence, during the 1980s a kind of doomsday scenario (analogous to similar doomsday extrapolations about energy needs and fossil fuels or about population increases) was projected by health administrators, economists and politicians.
In this scenario, ever-rising health costs were matched against static or declining resources.

orphan_explain_map.39: Q39: The passage talks about rising health costs and the need to decide how to share resources. But it never says whether OECD governments have **underestimated** the level of health-care provision needed. ***NOT GIVEN is not the same as FALSE*** — so the answer is **NOT GIVEN**.
orphan_explain_map.40: Q40: The passage mentions that elderly people are now major consumers of health-care. But it does not say anything about whether they will have to make **special provision** for their health-care in the future. ***Do not confuse a present fact with a future prediction*** — so the answer is **NOT GIVEN**.
